summary: The viewer is built to fall for the romance, dread the iceberg everyone knows is coming, feel the cold, and weep at the door and the whistle.

need-to-breathe.why: The flooding corridors and the plunge when the stern goes under are built to make the viewer hold breath.

hungry.why: Nothing is built to produce hunger.

full.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

thirsty.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

gassy.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

need-to-poop.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

need-to-pee.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

sleepy.why: The film does not aim to lull.

nauseous.why: Nothing is built to sicken the viewer.

urge-to-sneeze.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

urge-to-cough.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

dizzy.why: Rose over the stern rail, the flying at the bow, and the vertical stern are built to give the viewer vertigo.

fatigued.why: The viewer is not made to feel exertion.

pain.why: The water like a thousand knives, the funnel crushing swimmers, and Cal's slap are built to make the viewer wince.

disgusted.why: Cal's and Ruth's cruelty are built for moral distaste, nothing bodily.

itchy.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

tickled.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

over-stimulated.why: The sinking's roar and screams are loud but not built to overwhelm.

too-hot-too-cold.why: Frost on Jack's hair, the breath in the air, and the frozen dead are built to make the viewer feel the cold of the water.

afraid.why: The stern rising, the lights going out, and fifteen hundred in the water are built to frighten.

anxious.why: From the moment the iceberg is sighted the viewer is built to dread each stage of the sinking for Jack and Rose.

panic.why: The stampede for the boats and the race through flooding corridors are built to make the viewer's pulse race.

sensory-pleasures.why: The steerage dance, the wind at the bow, and the sunset are built as sensuous pleasure.

aesthetic-pleasures.why: The spectacle of the ship, the score, and the drawing scene are built for the viewer's pleasure in beauty.

piquancy.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

fun-excitement.why: The steerage party, the spitting lesson, and the bow are built as pure fun before the disaster.

orgasm.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

love-romantic.why: The film is built to make the viewer fall in love with Jack and Rose as they fall for each other, its central design.

love-family.why: The steerage mother tucking in her children and old Rose's photographs are built to touch family feeling.

grief.why: Jack's frozen hand slipping from Rose's and the whistle are built to make the viewer weep; the film is engineered for tears.

missing-someone.why: Old Rose's eighty-four years without Jack are built to make the viewer feel his absence.

aroused-sexually.why: The drawing scene and the handprint on the window are built to arouse, within a PG-13 frame.

liking-as-a-friend.why: The viewer is built to like Jack, Molly Brown, Fabrizio, and Tommy.

empathy.why: The viewer is placed with Rose from her first look at the ship, feeling her suffocation and her awakening.

compassion.why: The mother and children, the Strauses, the band, and the people in the water are built to produce pity.

grateful.why: Nothing is built to make the viewer grateful.

pleasure-from-helping.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

trustful-distrustful.why: The viewer watches Lovejoy plant the necklace and knows Jack is innocent while Rose doubts.

depressed.why: Nothing is built to lower the viewer's mood beyond grief.

angry.why: Cal's slap and the locked steerage gates are built to anger the viewer.

envious.why: Nothing is built to produce envy.

jealous-romantic-sexual.why: Nothing is built to make the viewer jealous.

jealous-friendship.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

hatred.why: Cal is built to be hated, from the breakfast table to the gun on the staircase.

contempt.why: Ruth's and Cal's snobbery and Ismay's vanity are built to draw the viewer's scorn.

resentment.why: The steerage gates and Cal's bribed seat are built to make the viewer feel class injustice.

proud.why: Nothing is built to make the viewer proud.

amused.why: Molly Brown's lines, the spitting lesson, and Jack at dinner are built for laughter.

sense-of-belonging.why: The viewer is recruited to steerage against first class at the party and the gates.

lonely.why: Rose's crowded-room speech and old Rose alone with her photographs are built to make the viewer feel isolation.

judgy-moral-sense.why: The viewer is built to judge Cal, Ruth, Ismay, and the lifeboat shortage, and to admire the band.

admiration.why: Jack's generosity, the band, Andrews, and Captain Smith at his post are built to be admired.

embarrassed.why: Jack fumbling the forks at dinner gives a flicker of secondhand embarrassment.

shame.why: Nothing is built to shame the viewer.

guilt.why: The lifeboats that do not go back may touch a viewer's conscience.

sad.why: The band's last hymn, the Strauses, the mother and children, and Jack's death are built to produce sorrow on a grand scale.

happy.why: The middle hour of romance is built to make the viewer happy before the iceberg.

joyful-euphoric.why: King of the world and flying at the bow are built as pure exhilaration.

effort.why: Three hours ask some patience, though the film is built to make them easy.

focused-in-flow.why: The sinking's last hour is built to hold the viewer rapt.

bored.why: The frame story's dives can drag a little, not by design.

impatient.why: The viewer knows the iceberg is coming and is built to wait for it through an hour of romance.

curious.why: The viewer wants to know what became of the diamond and how Rose survived.

surprised.why: Rose leaping back from the lifeboat and the diamond in old Rose's pocket are built to startle; the sinking is known.

awe.why: The ship of dreams in full, the stern standing vertical, and the sea of frozen dead are built to produce awe.

skeptical-doubtful.why: The viewer may doubt old Rose's story with Lovett's crew, briefly.

feeling-of-knowing.why: Old Rose recognizing the drawing on television is built to make the viewer feel a story about to surface.

frustrated.why: The door that fits only one, the lifeboat that will not turn back, and Rose's slow whistle are built to frustrate.

uncertain-certain.why: The viewer is certain the ship sinks and uncertain only who survives it.

understanding.why: The viewer understands Jack's saving of Rose in every way as old Rose names it.

inspired.why: Rose's promise to live fully is built to inspire the viewer.

satisfied.why: The diamond returned to the sea and the dream reunion close the film with a satisfaction it has earned through tears.

foreboding.why: Everyone knows the ship sinks, and the film plays on that knowledge from the first shot of the wreck.

nostalgia.why: Old Rose's narration and the restored ship are built to make the viewer feel the loss of 1912.

anticipation-suspense.why: The viewer waits for the iceberg, for Jack's chains to be cut, and for the whistle to be heard, suspense the film builds relentlessly.

hope.why: The viewer hopes the boats will come back and Jack will live, hopes the film grants and refuses.

schadenfreude.why: Cal's humiliation and his later suicide are built to be enjoyed.

elevation.why: The band playing on, the Strauses, and Jack giving Rose the door are built to lift the viewer.

infatuation.why: The viewer is built to share Rose's headlong falling for Jack.

rage.why: Cal with the gun may provoke a flash of rage in the viewer.
